title: Deploying and Observing the API
summary: Ship Roombook as a container image, configure it per environment, release it safely, and see inside it with logs, metrics, and traces.
intro: Roombook runs on your computer. Students can't book a room there. To be useful, it has to run on servers that stay up, get new versions without breaking the bookings people already made, and tell you when something goes wrong before a student does. That's the work of this last lesson: what deploying really involves, configuration that changes per environment, packing Roombook's Spring Boot code into a container image, running it behind a proxy with health checks, releasing a new version with its database migrations, and then seeing inside it with logs, metrics, and traces. It ends with what to watch after a release, and what you can build now that the course is done.

examples.title: Starting with a bad configuration
examples.prompt: Start Roombook with a five-letter JWT secret. The startup log is long, so `tail` keeps the last 12 lines, Spring's failure report.
examples.explanation: Spring Boot's **failure analyzer** turns the validation error into a report that names the property, where its value came from, and what was wrong, so you know to fix an environment variable and not a file. The application context never finished starting, so no port opened, and in a rolling deployment the new version never passes its first health check while the old one keeps serving. Notice that the report prints the rejected value. That's harmless for a five-letter test value, but it means a real secret that fails a check lands in the startup log, so treat that log as carefully as the secret store, and rotate a secret that ever appears in it.

steps.title: Containers and images, from zero
steps.body:
"It works on my machine" is the oldest problem in deploying. A server needs the right version of the runtime, the right system libraries, your code, and its dependencies, all in the right places, and every difference between your computer and the server is a chance to break. Containers solve that by shipping all of it together.

## What a container is

A **container** is an ordinary process on a Linux computer that the operating system walls off from everything else. Linux's **kernel**, the core of the operating system that runs every program, can give a process its own view of the world:

- its own **filesystem**, so it sees only the files it was given, not the server's,
- its own network address and ports, so two containers can both listen on 8080,
- its own list of processes, so it can't see or signal the others,
- limits on how much CPU and memory it may use.

Inside, the process thinks it has a small computer to itself. Outside, it's one more process, so a container starts in a fraction of a second and costs little more than the program inside it. A **virtual machine**, the older approach, pretends to be a whole computer with its own operating system, which is heavier and slower to start. On a Mac or Windows computer, Docker runs a small Linux virtual machine in the background to hold your containers.

## What an image is

An **image** is the template a container starts from: a read-only snapshot of a filesystem, holding the runtime, the libraries, and your code, plus a little metadata, like which command to run, which user to run it as, and which port it listens on. You build an image once, and any number of containers can start from it, on your computer, in CI, and in production, each with exactly the same files.

```diagram deploy-and-observe-image-layers
An image is a stack of read-only layers. Each container adds a thin writable layer of its own, which is lost when the container is removed.
```

An image is built in **layers**: each step of the build adds one, holding only the files that step changed. Layers are cached and shared, so when only your code changes, a rebuild reuses the layers below it, and a server that already has them downloads only the new one. That's why the order of a build's steps matters, as part 3 shows.

A running container adds a thin writable layer on top. Anything it writes there, like a file of uploads, disappears when the container is replaced, which happens on every deploy. That's the stateless rule from the scaling lesson, enforced: data lives in PostgreSQL, Redis, and MongoDB, and logs go to the terminal, where the platform collects them.

## Registries, tags, and digests

Images are stored in a **registry**: Docker Hub for public images, and GitHub's, AWS's, or Google's for private ones. An image's name has a **tag** after the colon, like `postgres:18` or `roombook-api:1.4.0`. A tag is a label that can move: `postgres:18` points at a newer image after each patch release. Every image also has a **digest**, like `sha256:4f1c...`, a fingerprint of its exact contents that never changes, so production can name the precise image staging tested.

## Docker

**Docker** is the most common tool for building images and running containers. A **Dockerfile** lists the steps that build an image, `docker build` runs them, and `docker run` starts a container. The data modeling lesson had you copy a command like the one in the example below, and now each part of it means something. Kubernetes, ECS, Cloud Run, Fly.io, and most platforms that run containers in production run the same images Docker builds, so everything here carries over.

examples.title: The docker run command, piece by piece
examples.prompt: The command the data modeling lesson used to run PostgreSQL on your computer, with a name and a volume added.
examples.code:
docker run --rm --name roombook-db \
  -p 5432:5432 \
  -e POSTGRES_USER=roombook -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=dev-only \
  -v roombook-pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql \
  postgres:18
examples.explanation: The last word is the image, `postgres:18`, which Docker downloads from Docker Hub the first time. `--rm` removes the container when it stops, and `--name` gives it a name for other commands, like `docker stop roombook-db`. `-p 5432:5432` publishes a port: the first number is on your computer, the second inside the container, so your code reaches the database at `localhost:5432`. Each `-e` sets an environment variable inside the container, which is how the image learns its user and password: the twelve-factor idea again. `-v` mounts a **volume**, storage Docker keeps outside the container, so the database's files survive when the container is removed. Without it, every restart would start from an empty database.

steps.title: Roombook's production image
steps.body:
A good production image is small, holds only what Roombook needs to run, and builds fast when only the code changed. Small matters for more than disk space: every tool left in an image is something an attacker could use, and something a vulnerability scanner will flag.

## Two stages

A **multi-stage** Dockerfile builds in two steps. The first stage, the **build stage**, has every tool the build needs. The second, the **runtime stage**, starts from a small base image and copies in only the result. The tools never reach production.

```diagram deploy-and-observe-build-stages
The build stage uses the JDK and Maven to build the jar and split it into layers. The runtime stage copies the layers onto a JRE.
```

For Spring Boot, the artifact is the executable jar that `./mvnw package` builds: your classes plus every dependency, about 31 MB here. Rather than copy that one file, Spring Boot can split it into **layers**, from the dependencies that rarely change to your own classes that change on every commit, and each becomes its own image layer, so a code change ships only the small one. The example below shows the jar and its layers.

## The Dockerfile

Roombook's `Dockerfile`, at the top of the project, uses Eclipse Temurin's images, with the full JDK to build and only the JRE, the Java runtime without the compiler, to run:

```dockerfile
FROM eclipse-temurin:25-jdk AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY mvnw pom.xml ./
COPY .mvn .mvn
RUN ./mvnw -q dependency:go-offline
COPY src src
RUN ./mvnw -q package -DskipTests \
 && java -Djarmode=tools -jar target/roombook-0.0.1-SNAPSHOT.jar extract --layers --launcher --destination extracted

FROM eclipse-temurin:25-jre
RUN useradd --create-home --uid 10001 roombook
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /app/extracted/dependencies/ ./
COPY --from=build /app/extracted/spring-boot-loader/ ./
COPY --from=build /app/extracted/snapshot-dependencies/ ./
COPY --from=build /app/extracted/application/ ./
USER roombook
EXPOSE 8080
ENV HOST=0.0.0.0 MANAGEMENT_SERVER_ADDRESS=0.0.0.0
ENV JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS="-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75"
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "org.springframework.boot.loader.launch.JarLauncher"]
```

`dependency:go-offline` downloads the dependencies from `pom.xml` alone, so that slow layer is reused until the dependencies change, and the tests have already run in CI. `extract --layers --launcher` unpacks the jar into the four layer folders, copied in order from least to most often changed. `JarLauncher` is Spring Boot's own entry point for an unpacked jar. The two `ENV` lines set environment variables in every container started from the image: the addresses to listen on, which part 4 explains, and the JVM's memory setting, below.

A few choices matter in every stack:

- **Pin the base image** to a version, never `latest`, so a rebuild next month gets the same foundation. Rebuild on a schedule anyway, to pick up security fixes in it.
- **Copy the dependency files first**, install, and only then copy the code. Docker reuses a cached layer until a file it copied changes, so a code change skips the slow install.
- **Run as a non-root user.** If an attacker gets code running inside the container, they get that user's powers, not root's.
- **Write a `.dockerignore`.** It lists files the build must never see, so `.env`, `.git`, and local build output stay out of the image:

```text
target
.env
.env.*
.git
.idea
```

## Build and run it

```bash
docker build -t roombook-api:1.4.0 .
docker run --rm -p 8080:8080 --env-file .env.docker roombook-api:1.4.0
```

`docker build` runs the Dockerfile in the current folder and tags the result. `docker run` starts a container with port 8080 inside published as 8080 on your computer, and `--env-file` passes a file of settings for your local test, which isn't baked into the image. `./mvnw spring-boot:build-image` is a second way to build an image with no Dockerfile at all, using Cloud Native Buildpacks, and it makes the same layers.

The image is tagged with its version, and the same name and tag go into the registry with `docker push`. The JVM sizes its memory from the container's limit, not the server's, and `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75` lets the **heap** use three quarters of it. The heap is the memory where your objects live, which the garbage collector from the first project lesson cleans up, and the last quarter is left for threads and the JVM itself. A container that goes over its limit is killed without a word, so watch memory after each release. Java 25 can also start from an **AOT cache**, AOT for ahead of time: a file, written during a practice run of the app, that holds its classes already loaded and linked, so each new container skips that work and rollouts go faster.

examples.title: The jar and its layers
examples.prompt: After `./mvnw package`, check the jar's size and list the layers Spring Boot can split it into.
examples.explanation: The jar is about 31 MB, almost all of it dependencies: Spring, Tomcat, Jackson, Micrometer, and the rest. `-Djarmode=tools` starts the jar in a special mode that inspects it instead of running Roombook, and `list-layers` prints its layers from the bottom up. `dependencies` holds the released libraries, `spring-boot-loader` the code that starts the app, `snapshot-dependencies` libraries still in development, and `application` your own classes and `application.yaml`. A typical commit changes only that last layer, a few hundred KB, which is all a server has to download for the new version.

steps.title: Proxies, health checks, and safe releases
steps.body:
An image on its own does nothing. It has to run somewhere that sends it traffic, restarts it when it's stuck, and replaces it with the next version without dropping a booking. This part sets up those three things, and the database changes that come with a release.

## Behind a reverse proxy

In production, Roombook never faces the internet directly. A **reverse proxy** or load balancer sits in front, as the scaling lesson described: it holds the TLS certificate, accepts HTTPS on port 443, enforces the body size limit from the security lesson, and forwards plain HTTP to Roombook's containers on the private network. Caddy is a proxy that gets and renews certificates by itself, and this is its whole configuration for Roombook:

```text
api.roombook.example {
    reverse_proxy roombook-api:8080
}
```

The first line is the site's name, which is all Caddy needs to get a certificate for it from Let's Encrypt, and `reverse_proxy` sends every request to Roombook's containers on the private network.

Two settings in Roombook change because of the proxy. First, inside a container, `127.0.0.1` means the container itself, so a server bound there can't be reached even by the proxy, and Roombook must listen on every address, `0.0.0.0`. Roombook's `application.yaml` reads the address from `HOST`, with `127.0.0.1` as the default for your own computer, as the first project lesson set up, so the Dockerfile sets `HOST=0.0.0.0`. Actuator's management port needs the same, and `MANAGEMENT_SERVER_ADDRESS=0.0.0.0` sets `management.server.address` through relaxed binding. The container's port is reachable only through the private network, so this is safe. Second, Roombook trusts the proxy's forwarded headers, and only the proxy's, as the security lesson set up.

## Health checks

The platform calls the health checks from the reliability lesson every few seconds, and names them **probes**: a failed liveness probe restarts the container, and a failed readiness probe takes it out of the load balancer until it passes again. Kubernetes adds a third kind, the **startup** probe, which gives a slow starter time before the other two begin. Roombook's probes are Actuator's `/actuator/health/liveness` and `/actuator/health/readiness`, on the management port, and readiness reports `OUT_OF_SERVICE` the moment graceful shutdown begins. In Kubernetes, the most common platform for containers, the probes are a few lines next to the image:

```yaml
# part of a Kubernetes Deployment
containers:
  - name: roombook-api
    image: registry.example/roombook-api:1.4.0
    ports:
      - containerPort: 8080
    startupProbe:
      httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/liveness, port: 9091 }
      periodSeconds: 2
      failureThreshold: 30
    livenessProbe:
      httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/liveness, port: 9091 }
      periodSeconds: 10
      failureThreshold: 3
    readinessProbe:
      httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/readiness, port: 9091 }
      periodSeconds: 5
```

The startup probe gives the container up to a minute, 30 tries two seconds apart, before the other two begin. After that, three failed liveness checks in a row restart it, and readiness is asked every five seconds.

## Migrations on deploy

A new version often needs a new column or table. The migrations from the lesson on raw SQL run as their own **release step**, after the image is built and before any new container starts, so the new code never meets an old schema. For Spring Boot, Flyway runs at startup by default, as the lesson on raw SQL set up, and it takes a lock so several instances starting at once can't run a file twice. As a release step, set `spring.flyway.enabled=false` in production and run the Flyway command line in the pipeline against the same files: `flyway -locations=filesystem:src/main/resources/db/migration migrate`, with the URL and credentials in `FLYWAY_URL`, `FLYWAY_USER`, and `FLYWAY_PASSWORD`.

The catch is that during a release, old and new versions run at the same time, against the same database. So a migration must work with both, and a breaking change takes several releases, a pattern called **expand and contract**. To rename a column: add the new column, release code that writes both and reads the new one, copy the old values across, and only in a later release drop the old column. Never drop or rename what the running version still uses.

## Rolling out, and rolling back

A **rolling deployment** replaces containers a few at a time:

```diagram deploy-and-observe-rollout
New containers start and pass readiness before old ones are drained, so the service never drops below full strength.
```

In step 1, the platform starts a container from the new image. In step 2, once its readiness probe passes, the load balancer adds it. In step 3, an old container is told to stop: its readiness fails at once, so no new requests arrive, and it finishes the ones in flight, the graceful shutdown from the reliability lesson. Then the next one goes. If the new containers never become ready, the rollout stops, with the old ones still serving.

**Rolling back** means deploying the previous image again, which takes a minute because nothing is rebuilt. That's only possible because the migrations were additive: the old code still works with the new schema. Migrations themselves only go forward, and a mistake in one is fixed by the next.

examples.title: Roombook and its databases in one file
examples.prompt: **Docker Compose** starts several containers from one file. This `compose.yaml`, next to the Dockerfile, runs the production image with PostgreSQL, Redis, and MongoDB, a production-shaped setup on your own computer. Start it with `docker compose up --build`.
examples.code:
# compose.yaml
services:
  api:
    build: .
    ports: ["8080:8080"]
    environment:
      SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL: jdbc:postgresql://db:5432/roombook
      SPRING_DATASOURCE_USERNAME: roombook
      SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD: dev-only
      SPRING_DATA_REDIS_URL: redis://redis:6379/0
      SPRING_MONGODB_URI: mongodb://mongo:27017/roombook
      ROOMBOOK_JWT_SECRET: dev-only-secret-change-me-0123456789abcdef
    depends_on:
      db: { condition: service_healthy }
      redis: { condition: service_started }
      mongo: { condition: service_started }
  db:
    image: postgres:18
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: roombook
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: dev-only
    volumes: ["pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql"]
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "pg_isready", "-U", "roombook"]
      interval: 5s
  redis:
    image: redis:8
  mongo:
    image: mongo:8.0
volumes:
  pgdata:
examples.explanation: Each entry under `services` becomes a container, and Compose puts them on one private network where each is reachable by its name, which is why the API's settings say `db`, `redis`, and `mongo` instead of `localhost`. `build: .` builds the image from the Dockerfile in this folder. The `healthcheck` runs `pg_isready` inside the database's container, and `depends_on` with `service_healthy` holds the API back until PostgreSQL answers, a small version of a readiness probe. The named volume `pgdata` keeps the database's files when its container is replaced. The `dev-only` values are for your own computer: in production, the platform injects real secrets, never a file in the repository. Flyway runs the migrations as the API starts, since this file leaves it on, which is fine for one instance on your own computer.

steps.title: Structured logs and metrics
steps.body:
Once Roombook runs on servers you can't see, the only way to know what it's doing is what it tells you. **Observability** is being able to answer new questions about a running system from the outside, like why bookings got slow at noon, and it rests on three kinds of signals: logs, metrics, and traces. This part covers the first two, and the next part the third.

## Structured logs

A **log** is the running story of what the service did, one event per line. Roombook writes **structured logs**: each line is a JSON object, with named fields instead of a sentence, so a log service can search and count them, like every 500 on `POST /v1/bookings` in the last hour, or every line with one request id.

Roombook writes its logs to standard output, the terminal, and nothing else. It doesn't open log files or send logs anywhere. The platform collects standard output from every container and ships it to a log service, like Grafana Loki, Elasticsearch, or a cloud's own, which is again the twelve-factor way.

Every line carries the same core fields: the time in UTC, a **level**, the message, the service and its version, and the request id from the middleware lesson. The level says how much the event matters: `debug` for detail you turn on while investigating, `info` for normal events like a finished request, `warn` for something odd that was handled, and `error` for a failure someone should look at. Production logs at `info`, and an environment variable, `LOGGING_LEVEL_ROOT=debug`, changes that without a new image, through relaxed binding. Each request writes one line when it finishes, with its route, status, and duration, and the security lesson's rule holds: ids and outcomes, never secrets.

Spring Boot writes structured logs by itself, with one setting in `application.yaml`. `ecs` is the Elastic Common Schema, a shared set of field names that most log services read:

```yaml
logging:
  structured:
    format:
      console: ecs
    ecs:
      service:
        version: ${APP_VERSION:dev}
```

Anything in the MDC, SLF4J's request-scoped map from the middleware lesson, becomes a field, so the request id filter's `requestId` lands on every line, and the line each request ends with, written here by a small `RequestLoggingFilter` beside the request id filter, adds its own fields with SLF4J's fluent API, `log.atInfo().addKeyValue("status", status)`. Here's one line from Roombook's log, laid out on several lines:

```json
{
  "@timestamp": "2026-11-22T00:09:45.282842Z",
  "log": { "level": "INFO", "logger": "dev.hackuniversity.roombook.config.RequestLoggingFilter" },
  "process": { "pid": 1855, "thread": { "name": "http-nio-127.0.0.1-8080-exec-1" } },
  "service": { "name": "roombook", "version": "1.4.0" },
  "message": "request completed",
  "requestId": "7f3a9c2e",
  "method": "GET",
  "route": "/v1/bookings/{id}",
  "status": 200,
  "durationMs": 36.2,
  "ecs": { "version": "8.11" }
}
```

`route` comes from the request attribute Spring MVC sets to the matched pattern, `HandlerMapping.BEST_MATCHING_PATTERN_ATTRIBUTE`. The first request after startup is the slowest, 36 ms here, while the JVM warms up its compiled code.

## Metrics

A **metric** is a number measured over time, like requests per second or the number of connections in use. Metrics are cheap to keep for months, since a counter costs the same whether it counted ten requests or ten million, and they're what dashboards and alerts are built on. There are three basic kinds:

- A **counter** only goes up, like requests served or bookings made. Graphs show its rate: how fast it grew per second.
- A **gauge** goes up and down, like connections in use or memory.
- A **histogram** counts observations into **buckets** by size, like how many requests took under 10 ms, under 25 ms, and so on.

Durations need histograms, because averages lie. If 99 requests take 20 ms and one takes 4 seconds, the average is 60 ms, which describes no request at all. A **percentile** says what most users saw: the **p95** is the time that 95 percent of requests beat, and the p99 shows the slow tail, where problems hide.

```diagram deploy-and-observe-histogram
Most requests land in the fast buckets, and the p99 marks the slow tail that an average hides.
```

Two short lists say what to measure. For anything that answers requests, **RED**: the **r**ate of requests, the **e**rrors, and their **d**uration. For resources like the connection pool, **USE**: **u**tilization, how busy it is, **s**aturation, how much work is waiting, and **e**rrors.

Each metric can carry **labels**, like the method, route, and status, and every new combination of label values is a new series to store. Label by the route's pattern, `/v1/bookings/{id}`, never by the real path or a user id, or the count of series, called the **cardinality**, explodes with every booking.

The common format is **Prometheus**, an open-source monitoring system that **scrapes** each container, fetching a `/metrics` page of plain text every 15 seconds or so. Roombook serves that page on the admin port from the security lesson, never on the public one. For Spring Boot, **Micrometer**, Spring's metrics library, already times every request as `http.server.requests`, with the method, the status, and the route's pattern as `uri`. The `micrometer-registry-prometheus` dependency adds the Prometheus format, and a few settings put it on the private port, with buckets that match Roombook's latency target, its SLO, which part 6 explains:

```yaml
management:
  server:
    port: 9091
  endpoints:
    web:
      exposure:
        include: health, prometheus
  metrics:
    distribution:
      slo:
        "[http.server.requests]": 5ms,10ms,25ms,50ms,100ms,250ms,500ms,1s,2500ms
```

The metric's name sits in quoted brackets, so YAML keeps its dots as part of the name instead of nesting it.

Micrometer also counts what the JVM, Tomcat, and HikariCP are doing, like heap use, threads, and connections in use and waiting, which is USE for the pool with no work at all. Spring Security covers the management port too, so its chain permits `/actuator/health/**` and `/actuator/prometheus`, which only the inside of the network can reach.

examples.title: Reading the histogram
examples.prompt: After a few requests for booking 1001, fetch the Prometheus page from the management port and keep the lines for that route's 200s.
examples.explanation: Each `_bucket` line counts the requests that took at most `le` seconds, "less than or equal", so the counts only grow down the list, and `+Inf` holds them all. Three requests finished within 5 ms, and the first, while the JVM warmed up, took longer, landing in the 50 ms bucket. `_count` is the number of requests and `_sum` their total time. `_max` is Micrometer's own extra: the slowest request recently seen. `outcome` and `exception` are labels Micrometer adds, with a handful of values each, so they don't hurt the cardinality.

steps.title: Traces, watching a release, and what's next
steps.body:
Logs say what happened, and metrics say how much. Neither says where the time went inside one slow request, which crossed the API, PostgreSQL, Redis, and a worker. Traces do, and with all three signals in place you can watch a release land and know whether it's good.

## Traces

A **trace** is the path of one request through every system it touches. It's made of **spans**: one span per operation, with a name, a start time, a duration, and a parent, so the spans nest into a tree. Drawn on a timeline, a trace is a **waterfall**:

```diagram deploy-and-observe-trace
One POST /v1/bookings: the handler's span holds the database and Redis spans, and the email worker's span joins the same trace later.
```

The handler's span is the whole request. Inside it, the transaction from the lesson on data integrity shows as its own span, with the insert inside that, and the cache delete from the Redis lesson follows. The email worker picks the job up later, from the outbox, and its span joins the same trace, because the trace id traveled with the job. One glance says whether a slow booking was slow in the database, in Redis, or in Roombook's own code.

**OpenTelemetry**, OTel for short, is the open standard for traces, and for metrics and logs too. Its libraries create spans for you around incoming requests, database queries, Redis commands, and outgoing HTTP calls, and send them to a collector, which forwards them to a tracing tool like Jaeger, Grafana Tempo, or a cloud's own. Between services, the trace id rides in a header called `traceparent`, so the next service's spans join the same trace. Roombook also puts it in the outbox row, so the worker can continue the trace.

Keeping every trace is expensive, so tools keep a sample, like one request in ten, plus every request that failed or was slow. Add the trace id to each log line, and a slow span leads you to its log lines, and a log line to its trace. For Spring Boot, Micrometer Tracing creates the spans, and an OpenTelemetry bridge sends them on. Spring Boot 4's OpenTelemetry starter brings both, and its settings live under `management.opentelemetry`:

```xml
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-opentelemetry</artifactId>
</dependency>
```

```yaml
management:
  tracing:
    sampling:
      probability: 0.1
  opentelemetry:
    tracing:
      export:
        otlp:
          endpoint: http://otel-collector:4318/v1/traces
```

Incoming requests and `RestClient` calls get spans, keeping one trace in ten, and the trace and span ids land in the MDC, so the structured log lines carry them with no more code. For a span around each SQL query, the `datasource-micrometer` library wraps the data source.

## Watching a release

The first hour after a release is when problems are cheapest to fix, so watch on purpose instead of hoping. A **service level objective**, an **SLO**, is the target you promise yourself, like 99.9 percent of booking requests succeeding, with 95 percent under 300 ms, over 30 days. The 0.1 percent it allows to fail is the **error budget**: while there's budget left, release freely, and when it's spent, slow down and fix things.

**Alerts** wake someone up, so they fire on what users feel, a rising error rate or a slow p95, not on causes like high CPU, which might not hurt anyone. After every release, compare the new version with the old, using the `version` field your logs and metrics carry:

- The error rate, and especially 5xx answers, per route.
- p95 and p99 latency, per route.
- Saturation: the connection pool, memory, CPU, and the queue behind the email worker.
- Restarts: a container that keeps failing its liveness probe.
- New kinds of error in the logs.
- Business numbers: bookings made per minute should look like last week's at this hour.

If any of them gets clearly worse, roll back first and investigate after. A rollback takes a minute, and finding the cause doesn't have to happen while students can't book rooms.

## What you can build now

You started this course with HTTP and Java, and you can now build an API from an empty folder to production: routes and validation, layered code, PostgreSQL in plain SQL with constraints and transactions, MongoDB where documents fit, sign-in with passwords, sessions, tokens, API keys, and OAuth, a documented and tested contract, caching, rate limits, queues, and reliable calls between services, and the security, deployment, and observability to run it for real. Roombook used all of it, and so can the next API you design.

Where to go next depends on what pulled at you. To run services at scale, learn Kubernetes and a cloud platform, and **infrastructure as code** with a tool like Terraform or OpenTofu, which describes servers and databases in files you review like code. To build the other side, the React and Next.js courses build a frontend for an API like this one. And the best next step is to build something of your own: a small API for a club, a game, or a problem you have, deployed and watched exactly as this lesson did.

recap:
- An environment is one running copy of the service, and only its configuration differs from the others.
- Build the artifact once and promote the same image to staging and production, configured from the environment and checked at startup.
- A container is an isolated process, and an image is the read-only layered template it starts from.
- A multi-stage Dockerfile keeps build tools out of production, and the image runs as a non-root user.
- Behind a reverse proxy, the app listens on 0.0.0.0, and liveness and readiness probes tell the platform when to restart it and when to send it traffic.
- Migrations run as a release step and expand before they contract, so old and new versions share the database safely.
- Structured JSON logs, RED metrics with histograms and low-cardinality labels, and traces with spans make the service observable.
- After a release, compare errors, latency, saturation, and business numbers by version, and roll back first if they get worse.
